styles.feasibility_notes: Build the logo from rects on an 8-pixel grid and use it as a clipPath over a tall stack of palette-coloured stripes that translates vertically in a CSS @keyframes loop with steps() timing; that is the raster split. Text bars are rects whose fill steps through 4-5 palette colours. The scroller is one group translated on X with the text duplicated for a seamless loop. No font can load, so define the 8x8 glyphs once as symbol elements and place them with use; about 60 glyphs costs a few KB. shape-rendering: crispEdges keeps the pixels hard.
styles.caveats: Do not copy any group name, logo shape or the Eagle Soft picture; the layout, raster split and block-letter technique are generic. Period scrolltexts often contain slurs (the Fairlight still shows one), so write new text. Dates are those shown on the intro screens and were not cross-checked on CSDb. Partly overlaps the 'SID title screen' part of the existing C64 style; keep this one strictly to the crack-intro layout.

styles.name: C64 DYCP demo part: sine-wave letters under a chunky multicolour logo
styles.era: 1989-1992, Commodore 64 demo scene (one-file demos, later crack intros)
styles.what_it_is: DYCP ("Different Y Character Position") is the C64 scroller in which every character sits at its own height, so a line of text ripples along a sine curve as it scrolls. It belongs with FLD (whole rows bouncing), tech-tech (each line of a logo shifted sideways) and sprites or scrollers in the opened border as the signature tricks of 1989-90.
visual_signature: A large two-row logo in multicolour character graphics with double-wide pixels, each letter filled with diagonal or vertical colour stripes in 3-4 palette steps and a dark outline (Sphinx: diagonal rainbow stripes)
The logo sits on a mauve panel made of thin horizontal stripes, closed above and below by grey/white raster rules
Text whose letters each ride a sine wave, forming an arc or U shape under the logo (The Force: letters hanging in a U beneath a two-row logo, yellow top row, blue-grey metallic bottom row)
A small static credit line in a second colour ('CODE BY ... MUSIC BY ...') at the very top
A straight one-line message in a gold gradient font between logo rows
Optional open-border variant: the scroller or sprites run in the top and bottom border area, outside the 320x200 picture
styles.palette: C64 16-colour palette on black. Logo fills use luminance ramps (blue, light blue, cyan, white; brown, orange, yellow, white). Multicolour mode means 160 double-wide pixels across, so logo edges step in 2-pixel units.
styles.typography: Logo: fat squared capitals about 4-5 character cells high. Scroller: 8x8 custom capitals, one colour per character, sometimes with a raster colour wash.
styles.motion: Each letter moves up and down on a sine table, offset in phase from its neighbour, while the whole line scrolls left. FLD: the entire logo bounces vertically. Tech-tech: each scanline of the logo slides horizontally. Motion comes from written descriptions, not from watching.

references.what: DYCP Mania by Sphinx, 20 May 1989, Venlo Meeting (code, graphics and charset ABS 3001): striped logo on mauve panels
DYCP Intro by The Force (1991, C64 crack intro, code Nir P.): scroller arcing under the logo
DYCP in 1992 by Chaos-Front (March 1992, one-file demo, code and charset Nuke)
DYCP Part by The Falcons (one-file demo, code Griper, graphics X-Port; undated on CSDb)
Plus/4 World encyclopedia: definition and expansion of DYCP, MegaDYCP and DYSCP
Wikipedia on C64 demo techniques: FLD, FLI, tech-tech ('Tec-Tec'), sprite multiplexing, sprites in the opened border
Albert of Pu-239 on his own 1989 parts: FLD bounce, a border-breaking sinus scroll, a sprite tech-tech

styles.readme_translation: Above the fold: an animated SVG with the project name as the striped logo on a mauve panel and the tagline as the DYCP line beneath it. Keep the wave amplitude modest (8-12 pixels at 1x) so the line stays readable. Stats or section names go in the static credit line. Links sit in Markdown below.
styles.feasibility_notes: Each glyph is a use of an 8x8 symbol inside its own group with a CSS translateY animation (animation-direction: alternate, timing cubic-bezier(0.37,0,0.63,1), which is a near-exact sine) and a negative animation-delay that grows per character. One translateX animation on the parent scrolls the line; duplicate the text and make the per-glyph phase repeat over the text length so the loop is seamless. 40-80 animated glyphs is well within budget. FLD is one translateY on the logo group. Tech-tech is the logo cut into 1-row clip strips with staggered translateX. The open-border variant is only a drawn C64 border frame with the scroller placed over it.
styles.caveats: Do not copy the group logos or their charsets; sine text and striped block letters are generic. No source opened says who did DYCP first, so make no such claim. Moving text is harder to read, so repeat the real information as static text. The open-border variant loses its meaning outside a real screen and only reads as a C64 in-joke.

styles.name: PETSCII picture: C64 text-mode art on the 40-column grid
styles.era: Character set used on the C64 from 1982; a demoscene art form in its own right since Marq's PETSCII editor of September 2013
styles.what_it_is: Pictures and logos built only from the C64's built-in character set: 40x25 cells, each an 8x8 glyph in one foreground colour over a single shared background colour. Tommi Musturi's article says it was first used for floppy directory art, BBS graphics and beginners' BASIC programs, and that competitions and dedicated demos came only after the editor made it available to everyone.
visual_signature: A visible 8x8 cell grid: edges are horizontal, vertical or 45-degree diagonals, because those are the shapes the glyph set offers
One background colour for the whole picture, plus one colour per cell
Solid blocks, half and quarter blocks, diagonal wedges, line and corner glyphs, and the checkerboard glyph for the little dithering that works
Reverse-video cells used to double the glyph set (128 glyphs plus 128 inverses)
Deliberately visible colour clashes between neighbouring cells, giving a comic-strip look
A wide single-colour border around the 320x200 picture area (light violet in the 2026 example viewed, which shows a lawn, trees, two seated figures and a computer on a table)
Lettering made from the same glyphs: ROM capitals, or large letters assembled from block and wedge cells 3-5 cells tall
styles.palette: The 16 fixed C64 colours; one global background plus one colour per cell. The example viewed uses a bright green ground, light violet sky and border, with yellow, brown, black and white on top.
styles.typography: C64 ROM character set (uppercase plus graphics symbols). Big letters are mosaics of block, wedge and line glyphs.
styles.motion: Usually static. When animated it is cell changes frame by frame (a blinking cursor, colour cycling on a few cells, a two-frame character swap), never smooth movement.

references.what: Tommi Musturi, 'Unplanned Blocky Puzzles: Creating PETSCII for the Commodore 64' (WiderScreen, 2017): constraints, global-colour strategy, dithering limits, history of use
Marq's PETSCII editor on CSDb (Fit, 28 September 2013; help from Dr. TerrorZ)
C64-Wiki on the editor: 40x25 with 16 colours, a 16x25 dir-art mode, export formats
PETSCII Picnic by Daimansion of Excess (15 August 2026, 4th in mixed graphics at BREAKOUT 2026): a recent competition picture

styles.readme_translation: Above the fold: a static or lightly animated SVG on a 40-column grid, 12-16 rows tall so it works as a banner: project name in block-glyph letters, a small scene or mascot built from cells, a coloured border. A caption line in ROM-style capitals gives the tagline. Body text and links stay in Markdown.
styles.feasibility_notes: Define each glyph used as an 8x8 symbol (runs of rects), place cells with use and a fill colour, draw the background as one rect, set shape-rendering to crispEdges. 40x14 cells is 560 elements, roughly 30-40 KB. A few cells can swap or change colour with steps() keyframes. The technique is easy; drawing a good picture within it is the hard part, so a generator should offer block-letter titles and a small library of original cell motifs. A pure-text version is not dependable: Unicode's Symbols for Legacy Computing block has PETSCII-like glyphs but common monospace fonts lack them, so only ordinary block and box-drawing characters are safe on GitHub.
styles.caveats: Do not trace or copy anyone's PETSCII picture. The glyph shapes come from Commodore's ROM font; redraw equivalent 8x8 shapes instead of ripping the font. Low-contrast C64 pairs (blue on black, brown on black) fail contrast checks, so put text on strong pairs. Wow depends heavily on the picture; a title-only banner is a 3.

styles.name: C64 disk directory art (dir art)
styles.era: C64 floppy disks from the 1980s onward; still made, with tools and competition entries on CSDb dated 2019-2026
styles.what_it_is: Art drawn inside a 1541 disk directory listing: when the disk is listed, the file names themselves form a picture or a framed title. It works because directory listings on a C64 are unsorted and the directory blocks are simple enough to edit by hand, so an artist can fill the 16-character name column with PETSCII graphics row after row. Unlike the existing boot/loader style, the listing itself is the canvas.
visual_signature: A reverse-video header line: a zero, the disk name in quotes, then a short ID (in the example viewed the ID slot carries the artist's tag)
Every following row has three columns: a block count on the left (usually 0), a quoted 16-character name, and a file type on the right (PRG or DEL)
The art lives only in the 16-character name column, so the picture is a narrow vertical strip 16 cells wide and as many rows tall as needed
Line-drawing and block glyphs form a framed title, big outline lettering and a small scene (the example shows a title in double-line letters, a crane, two rooftops and a standing figure)
A footer line: a number followed by BLOCKS FREE.
One colour only: light blue-violet text on a darker blue-violet screen, the default C64 colours
A signature in the last name row
styles.palette: Monochrome by nature: default C64 light blue (6C5EB5) on blue (352879). As README text it takes the reader's theme colours.
styles.typography: C64 ROM capitals and PETSCII line, corner and block glyphs; fixed 16-character name field; the quotes around each name are part of the look.
styles.motion: static

references.what: Canabalt DirArt by Logiker (13 October 2019, released at Vintage Computing Carinthia $02): full example with header, PRG/DEL column and blocks-free footer
Championship Wrestling +3D DirArt (Excess, 24 February 2019; concept Faayd and Logiker, directory art Logiker; 3rd in C64 graphics at BCC Party #13)
C64 OS blog on why directory art works: PETSCII symbols, a simple unvalidated directory structure, unsorted listings
CSDb search for 'dirart': 21 releases including the tools Dirarter, DART Directory Art Importer and Txt2dirart

styles.readme_translation: Entirely text in a pre block. The header line is the project name, each 'file' row is either a row of the picture or a real entry (a section name that can be a link inside the pre), the left column carries real numbers (item counts, sizes), and the footer is a stat line. Illustration of the row structure, my own: a header such as 0 "FACTORY TOOLS   " 2A, rows such as 140  "ITEMS"  PRG and 0  "+--------------+"  DEL, then 477 BLOCKS FREE. An optional SVG twin can add the blue screen.
styles.feasibility_notes: About 30 columns wide, far below 80. Use only box-drawing and block characters every monospace font has. GitHub's pre line spacing leaves small gaps in vertical strokes, so designs built from horizontal strokes and solid blocks survive better than tall thin frames. Anchor tags inside the pre make name rows clickable. Reverse video for the header is not available in plain text; mark it with a rule line or bold instead.
styles.caveats: Do not copy an existing directory picture; the listing format is a machine convention and free to imitate. Do not reproduce Commodore's startup banner wording as branding. Screen readers read the rows character by character, so put a plain-text summary under it. This is the only pure-text style in this family, which is its main value.

styles.name: Razor 1911 Amiga cracktro (Sector9, 1990-91): logo plate, deep-blue panel, rainbow copper text
styles.era: 1990-1991, Amiga OCS; cracktros and text screens by the Norwegian group's Amiga section, mostly credited to Sector9
styles.what_it_is: Razor 1911 began on the C64 in 1985 as Razor 2992 and moved to the Amiga in 1987-88, before its PC years. Pouet lists about fifteen Amiga cracktros from 1989 to 1994. 'Birds of Prey' (December 1991, code and graphics Sector9, with Sim; music 'Necroscope' by Mantronix) is the one commenters call "a great famous crack intro by the REAL razor 1911", praising its chiptune and "wavy colour cycling with the swirling letters". It is a sub-variant of the existing Amiga cracktro: no starfield and no copper-bar stack, but a framed two-panel layout in which the text itself carries the colour.
visual_signature: Two stacked panels on black, separated by thin light-blue rules: a short mid-grey strip on top, a tall deep navy panel below
In the grey strip, a small logo plate: a dark rounded capsule with a chrome rim holding the group name in red outlined capitals with a white highlight, and a small bar ornament either side
In the navy panel, 3 lines of wide, slanted, rounded capitals whose fill is a horizontal rainbow running red, orange, yellow, green, cyan, blue across the line
Dashed rules above and below the text made of short segments coloured in the same rainbow order
Small four-point star sprites in light blue at both ends of the first text line

Text-page variant (Rolling Ronny, July 1991; Vertical Insanity, 1990): a full dark-blue screen of tightly packed 8-pixel capitals in blocks separated by dashed rules (title, supplied by / cracked by, contacts in two columns, greetings), each block tinted a different colour (magenta, white, orange, light blue)

Black-screen variant (Renegade Legion Interceptor, May 1991): centred blue-gradient serif text lines between '--=))' and '((=--' ornaments, red chrome letters that spin into place, and a one-line orange-gradient scroller on a navy band with thin rules at the bottom
styles.palette: Amiga 12-bit colour. Navy panel (about 002 to 005 in 12-bit terms), mid-grey strip, light-blue rules, a full-hue rainbow for the text, red with white highlights for the logo. The text-page variant uses magenta, white, orange and light blue on dark blue.
styles.typography: Wide slanted rounded capitals about 16 pixels high for the rainbow lines; an 8-pixel capitals font for the text pages; a heavy red outlined wordmark with white highlights for the logo. All hand-pixelled by the group's own artists (Pouet and Demozoo credit Sector9 and, for one logo, Insane TTM).
styles.motion: The rainbow cycles along the text and the lines wave; commenters describe swirling letters. In the black-screen variant letters rotate into place and a scroller runs at the bottom. Text pages are static apart from colour cycling. Motion is from comments, not from watching.

references.what: Birds of Prey cracktro on Pouet (December 1991): still with logo plate and rainbow text; comments on its fame, the Mantronix chiptune and the wavy colour cycling
Birds of Prey on Demozoo: 7 December 1991; Sector 9 code and graphics, Sim code, Mantronix music ('Necroscope')
Rolling Ronny cracktro (July 1991, graphics Sector9): the dense colour-tinted text page
Renegade Legion Interceptor cracktro (May 1991, code Sector9): blue gradient text, red chrome letters, bottom scroller band
Vertical Insanity (August 1990): the plain blue text screen with credits and board numbers; comments describe a vertical copper rainbow
Pouet's Razor 1911 group page: the list of Amiga cracktros, intros and demos 1988-1995
Demozoo's Razor 1911 group page: history notes (C64 start, Amiga reform in 1987, shift to PC around 1991)
Wikipedia on Razor 1911: founded October 1985 in Norway as Razor 2992; C64, then Amiga, then PC

styles.readme_translation: Above the fold: an animated SVG about 800x300. Top strip with the project name in a capsule plate; navy panel with three rainbow lines: project name, PRESENTS, the one-line description; dashed rainbow rules and two star sprites. Under it, the text-page variant as a real pre block: title, 'supplied by / built by', contacts, greetings, which doubles as the README's info section with working links.
styles.feasibility_notes: Rainbow text: pixel-glyph shapes as a clipPath over a wide horizontal linearGradient with hard stops (12-bit steps), twice the panel width and translated on X in a loop so the colours cycle. The wave: cut each line into per-glyph groups with translateY, alternate direction, cubic-bezier(0.37,0,0.63,1) and staggered negative delays. Dashed rules are short rects with the same gradient. Stars are 5-rect sprites with an opacity blink. The logo plate is a rounded rect with a stepped gradient rim. The text page needs no SVG at all.
styles.caveats: This is the reference most at risk of becoming an imitation: do not use the Razor 1911 name, the numerals, the capsule wordmark or its letterforms, and do not imitate their release wording as if the project were theirs. The reusable parts are the two-panel frame, rainbow-filled wavy text and dashed rules. The owner may have meant the PC-era Razor intros, which are a different look and another family. Rainbow colour cycling is a motion and contrast risk; keep it slow and add a prefers-reduced-motion rule. Period text pages carry phone numbers and postal addresses; never reproduce them.

styles.name: Amiga megademo menu and trainer menu: chrome logo, giant scroller, dotted-leader option list
styles.era: 1989-1990 for megademos (Red Sector, Kefrens, Alcatraz); 1989 onward for trainer menus in front of cracked games
styles.what_it_is: Two related Amiga list screens. A megademo was a disk of separate parts by different coders tied together by a loader screen with a part list: Red Sector's Megademo (9 September 1989, first at the Tristar Party) and Kefrens' Megademo VIII (18 February 1990, first at the Kefrens and Dexion Party). A trainer menu is the screen a cracking group put before a game, asking which cheats to enable. Both differ from the existing copper-bar cracktro by being structured lists with a selection.
visual_signature: Black screen with a sparse field of single-pixel white stars
A wide chrome logo across the top: blue at the top of the letters, a bright white horizon band, grey below (Kefrens Megademo 8 menu)
A small spaced-capitals subtitle under the logo in light blue
One very large scroller, plain white block capitals about a fifth of the screen high, crossing the middle

A centred list headed by a dashed title line ('- SELECT DEMO TO WATCH -'), then rows of 'PART NAME......CODER' with dotted leaders, tinted by a vertical gradient from blue through violet to pink so each row is a different shade
A last row that leads to the next disk's menu
Trainer variant: rows of 'UNLIMITED LIVES ........ NO' (or OFF), a title in a solid blue band, a full-width yellow bar marking the 'START THE GAME' row, all text in one colour on black
Trainer background: dotted sine curves or a handful of drifting dots, no pictures
styles.palette: Amiga OCS 12-bit colour, 16 steps per channel, so gradients band finely. Black, white stars, a blue-white-grey chrome logo, a list gradient from mid blue through violet to pink, one accent bar (yellow or blue) for the selection.
styles.typography: Logo: heavy squared capitals, hand-pixelled, with horizontal banding. List text: small 8-pixel capitals with wide spacing and dotted leaders. Scroller: block capitals 32 pixels or taller. The fonts in these specific screens were not identified.
styles.motion: Stars drift in two or three speed layers; the giant scroller moves right to left; in the trainer variant the highlight bar steps from row to row and the values flip. Inferred from stills and general descriptions, not watched.

references.what: Kefrens Megademo 8 on Pouet: menu still with logo, big scroller and the 'select demo to watch' list (entry credits Mellica for code and graphics)
Megademo VIII on Demozoo: 18 February 1990, first at the Kefrens and Dexion Party, eight coders credited, tags copper-wall and glenz-vector
Red Sector Megademo on Demozoo: 9 September 1989, first at Tristar Party 1989, full credits
Red Sector Megademo on Pouet: title still and comments naming the vectorballs part
Alcatraz 'Bones Brigade trainer' (1989): blue title band, option rows with NO values, yellow bar on START THE GAME, dotted sine curves
Alcatraz 'Black Tiger +6 Trainer' (1989): six option rows with OFF values in blue on black
Wikipedia on trainers: built into the cracked game, shown first, asking which cheats to enable; plus signs in release names, one per option

styles.readme_translation: Above the fold: an animated SVG with the project name as the chrome logo over a starfield and the tagline as the giant scroller. The list becomes the table of contents: section name, dotted leader, a value on the right (a count, a version). The trainer variant suits feature flags: 'OFFLINE MODE ........ YES'. Image text cannot be a link, so repeat the list as a linked pre block under the image; the dotted-leader list works as plain text on its own.
styles.feasibility_notes: Stars: 1-pixel rects in three groups translated at different speeds, each group duplicated one screen-width along for a seamless wrap. Chrome logo: pixel letters as a clipPath over a linearGradient with paired hard stops to keep the banding. List gradient: one vertical gradient applied through a mask of the glyphs. Selection bar: a rect moved with steps() keyframes; the value flip is two overlapping glyph groups toggling opacity. The text list is a pre block with period leaders padded to a fixed column.
styles.caveats: Do not copy the Kefrens, Red Sector or Alcatraz names or logo shapes, or the sunglasses face in the Red Sector title. The list structure, starfield and chrome treatment are generic. It shares the chrome logo and starfield with the existing Amiga cracktro, so only the list and the giant scroller make it distinct; hence wow 3. 'Trainer' wording on a legitimate project is a joke some readers will not get.

styles.name: Vertical copper bars ('Kefrens bars' / 'Alcatraz bars'): ribbons twisting down the screen
styles.era: 1989-1991 on Amiga; seen on the Atari ST by 1991
styles.what_it_is: A one-trick Amiga effect: shaded vertical bars that sway left and right as they descend, leaving a woven ribbon pattern. It is made by showing a single line of video memory on every scanline and drawing a new bar into that line as the beam moves down. It carries Kefrens' name, but a Pouet commenter (hitchhikr) says it was invented by Metalwar of Alcatraz in 'We are first' in Megademo 3 (February 1989).
visual_signature: Vertical bars: each a narrow column 8-16 pixels wide with a rounded shading ramp, dark edges and a bright centre
Each bar starts at its own scanline and runs to the bottom, so later bars overlap earlier ones and the top of the screen is emptier than the bottom
Bar positions follow a sine from one scanline to the next, giving S-curves and braided ribbons
Visible one-line steps along the curves, because a bar can only shift by whole pixels
Black background; bars in two or three hues
Usually paired with a very large scroller in front; in Alcatraz Megademo 3 the big letters are built from a grey stone-block texture
Atari ST version: yellow and blue stepped bars spinning over a red-to-black scanline gradient, with letters made of dots rotating in front (Pompey Pirates Menu 001 V2)
styles.palette: Amiga 12-bit colours in ramps of 5-8 steps per bar, for example dark red to yellow to white and back, or deep blue to cyan to white. Commenters describe Razor 1911's 'Vertical Insanity' as a vertical copper rainbow.
styles.typography: None of its own; paired with a large block-capital scroller.
styles.motion: The whole ribbon pattern swings and twists continuously as the sine phases advance. Steady and hypnotic, not fast. Not watched; taken from the technique description and comments.

references.what: Alcatraz Megademo 3 (February 1989) on Pouet: hitchhikr calls it the first vertical 'copper' bars; another commenter lists a giant scroller with vertical bars among the parts
Razor 1911 'Vertical Insanity' (August 1990): comments on the vertical copper rainbow, and hitchhikr's attribution to Metalwar of Alcatraz
Sol's graphics tutorial chapter on the effect: one line of framebuffer repeated down the screen and changed as the display is drawn; the author says he does not know the exact history
Wikipedia's demo effect article, which lists Kefrens bars as vertical raster bars
Pompey Pirates Menu 001 V2 (Atari ST, November 1991): the spinning vertical bars behind a game menu; a commenter compares them to the Cuddly Demos reset screen

styles.readme_translation: Above the fold: an animated SVG banner, wide and short (for example 800x200), with the ribbon filling the background and the project name in large block capitals in front on a dark plate so it stays readable. All information text stays outside the effect.
styles.feasibility_notes: Reproduce the real mechanism. For each of 60-100 scanline rows k, draw one rect that starts at row k and runs to the bottom, filled with a shared horizontal shading gradient, and animate its X with translateX (alternate, cubic-bezier(0.37,0,0.63,1)) using a negative delay proportional to k. Later rects paint over earlier ones, which gives the correct overlap for free. Nest a second group with a slower animation for the sum of two sines. About 100 animated elements and two gradients is a few KB.
styles.caveats: The effect is a generic technique; do not attach the Kefrens, Alcatraz or Razor 1911 names to it as branding. The origin claim rests on one commenter repeated on two Pouet pages and should be presented as that. Continuous swaying across the full width can be uncomfortable: add a prefers-reduced-motion rule that freezes the ribbon.

styles.name: Bobs and dot objects: a sphere chain on a Lissajous path, a rotating dot cube
styles.era: 1989-1990, Amiga OCS; 'bobs' are blitter-drawn sprites, the staple effect of early Amiga intros
styles.what_it_is: A black screen with one moving object made of many identical pieces: a chain of shaded balls snaking along a figure-eight, or a lattice of dots rotating in space, above a logo strip. Razor 1911's 'Liquid Bobs' (3rd at the IT, Rawhead, The Band and IMP-666 Megaparty 1989) and 'Space Dots' (January 1990) are compact examples, and Pouet commenters single out the vectorballs part of Red Sector's Megademo.
visual_signature: About 30 shaded spheres in one hue (blue with a white highlight dot at upper left) strung along a figure-eight or infinity-shaped curve
Sphere size varies along the chain, large near the viewer and small far away, so the loop reads as three-dimensional
A lattice of single white-blue dots forming a box in perspective, rows of dots converging to one side (Space Dots)
The effect area is closed above and below by a one-pixel horizontal rule whose colour runs through a rainbow from left to right
A logo strip at the bottom: wide pixel capitals filled with a vertical gradient (violet to cyan in Space Dots; red over blue chrome with a white horizon in Liquid Bobs)
Nothing else: black background, no starfield, no picture
styles.palette: Black; one ball colour in a 4-5 step ramp from dark blue to white; a rainbow hairline; a two-colour gradient logo. Amiga 12-bit steps.
styles.typography: Only the logo strip: geometric pixel capitals 24-32 pixels high with gradient fill; Archmage's Pouet comment on Space Dots praises the font.
styles.motion: The chain travels along its curve, each ball following the one ahead; the curve itself slowly changes shape as the two sine frequencies drift. The dot box rotates. Shade bobs, a later relative in which overlapping bobs brighten the pixels beneath them (Demozoo's earliest tagged examples are December 1991), leave trails that cannot be reproduced without scripts.

references.what: Liquid Bobs by Razor 1911 on Pouet: still of the blue sphere chain with logo strip; Pouet dates it January 1989
Liquid Bobs on Demozoo: dated 26 March 1989; Doctor No code, Sector 9 code and charset, Insane TTM the Razor logo, Hattrick music; tag 'bobs'
Space Dots by Razor 1911 (January 1990, code and graphics Sector9): dot lattice between rainbow rules, gradient logo
Red Sector Megademo on Pouet: comments naming the vectorballs part
Demozoo's shade-bobs tag: earliest entries are Anarchy's '3D Demo' and 'Hardwired' by Crionics and The Silents, both December 1991

styles.readme_translation: Above the fold: an animated SVG about 800x260. The sphere chain loops in the upper two thirds between two rainbow hairlines; the project name is the gradient logo strip at the bottom; a one-line tagline in small pixel capitals sits under it. For a factory tool the balls could be items riding the curve like a conveyor. All other text is Markdown.
styles.feasibility_notes: A Lissajous path needs no script: nest two groups per ball, the outer animating translateX and the inner translateY, each alternate with cubic-bezier(0.37,0,0.63,1) and different durations (for example 4s and 2s gives a figure-eight). Give each of 30 balls a negative delay offset to form the chain. A third nested animation on scale, a quarter period out of phase, gives depth. Each ball is a circle with one shared radialGradient using hard stops. A dot lattice rotating about the vertical axis is exact in the same way: each dot's X is a sine of time with its own amplitude and phase, and opacity follows a second sine for depth. Z-order cannot change during the loop, a small inaccuracy. 30 balls or 60 dots is a few KB.
styles.caveats: Do not copy the Razor 1911 logo strips or names; balls on a sine path and dot lattices are generic. The two databases disagree on the Liquid Bobs date and credits, as shown. Only stills were seen, so the motion description is inferred. True shade bobs and filled or glenz vector objects are not achievable without scripts beyond a few pre-computed frames.

styles.name: Copper-only screen: full-screen colour fields with no bitmap at all
styles.era: 1990-1991, Amiga OCS
styles.what_it_is: Screens drawn with the Amiga's copper alone: the display list changes the background colour every scanline and several times along each line, so the picture is pure colour with no pixels behind it. Angels' 'Copper Master' and Razor 1911's 'Look! No bitplanes' were both released at the No Limits and IMP-666 party in October 1990. Plasma, which Wikipedia notes was particularly common on the Amiga because it could be done very efficiently there, is the best-known relative.
visual_signature: Soft diagonal bands sweeping across the whole screen in three or four ramps (green, brown, blue, white)
A diamond of nested colour: red at the edges through orange and yellow to a blue core, mirrored top to bottom and left to right
A plaid of overlapping vertical and horizontal bars in pure red, green and blue whose crossings mix to yellow, cyan and magenta
A twisted ribbon made of thin alternating red and grey stripes over a field of cyan horizontal lines
Colour changes only in chunky steps along a line (cells several pixels wide) but on every scanline vertically, so the texture is wide and short
Each effect shown in a bordered window with a thin light frame; no logo art, at most a plain text title
In 'Look! No bitplanes': a big red wordmark with jagged serifs and blue chrome lines of text on black, plus what a commenter calls a copper starfield
styles.palette: The whole 12-bit range at once: fully saturated red, green and blue and their mixes, in ramps of 16 steps per channel. A Pouet commenter on Copper Master says he had not seen so many colours in a long while.
styles.typography: Minimal. Copper Master credits Mistervideo for font and design (Demozoo: Mr. Video, charset); titles are plain capitals.
styles.motion: Bands roll, the diamond pulses outward, plaid bars slide across each other, the ribbon twists. Plasma-style movement comes from summing sine waves and cycling the palette. Copper Master's coder commented that matching the colours to Moby's music took a long time. Not watched; from stills and written sources.

references.what: Copper Master by Angels on Pouet (October 1990; code Corsair, font and design Mistervideo, music Moby): four stills and comments calling it a 'copper overdose'
Copper Master on Demozoo: 6 October 1990, No Limits and IMP-666 Amiga Conference; note that Corsair later made a similar-looking crack intro for Angels
Look! No bitplanes by Razor 1911 (October 1990, 3rd at the same party; code Nosferatu, graphics Sector9)
Madness by Anarchy (17 October 1990, tagged plasma on Demozoo; not viewed, listed as a dated plasma example only)
Wikipedia on the plasma effect: summed sine waves, palette cycling, common on the Amiga

styles.readme_translation: Above the fold: an animated SVG banner that is nothing but moving colour, with the project name in large solid capitals (black or white with a dark outline) on top and a one-line tagline. It carries its own background, so it works in light and dark themes. Everything informative is Markdown below.
styles.feasibility_notes: Rolling bands: a stack of 2-pixel-high rects sharing one fill animation through a 16-step palette, each row with a negative delay proportional to its row number. Plaid: two groups of gradient-filled bars, one vertical and one horizontal, translated in opposite directions with mix-blend-mode: screen on the upper group (or an feBlend filter). Plasma: a grid of about 40x12 cells; precompute a sum-of-sines value per cell, quantise it to 16 or 32 levels, give every cell of one level the same class, and run one colour-cycle animation per class with the delay set by the level. That is palette cycling and needs no script; 480 rects is about 20 KB. Keep cells 8 pixels wide and 2-4 tall for the copper look.
styles.caveats: The effects are generic; do not reuse the group names or the Razor wordmark. Full-screen saturated colour cycling is the biggest accessibility risk in this family: keep cycles slower than about one per 3 seconds, avoid red flashing, and freeze it under prefers-reduced-motion. Text over it needs a solid plate or heavy outline to stay legible. I did not confirm that 'Look! No bitplanes' contains a plasma, so none is claimed for it.

styles.name: Melon Dezign: flat colour fields, stepped silhouettes, curved black text
styles.era: November 1991 onward, Amiga; the classic run is 1992-93, including cracktros made for the cracking group Crystal (Denmark and France)
styles.what_it_is: Melon Dezign was founded by Paleface and Seen after they left Quartex, at first as the demo and intro arm of Crystal. Their intros replaced chrome and starfields with flat colour, simple shapes and graphic-design layout. A Pouet commenter says 'Human Target' (1st at the Easter Conference, April 1992) "totally changed the way demos were designed". It is the clearest break from the look the existing six styles share.
visual_signature: Large areas of flat, unshaded colour: in the 'Zool' cracktro three stacked bands, hot pink, mustard yellow and mid green
Band edges cut as stepped rectangles like a city skyline, with no outline between colours
Black bold capitals set along a wavy curve across the bands, each letter rotated to follow it, with a small offset shadow ('... proudly presents')
Concentric rings in two flat colours (orange on violet in 'Mind Expanding') behind solid black silhouettes of two standing people
A tiny group tag in a top corner: lower-case letters in a small box, half white-on-black and half black-on-white
A muted grey-blue field with two thin horizontal rules and small centred text in bright green, credits written with dotted leaders ('Graphics & Design...............Seen')
A grid of identical cubes coloured across the hue range row by row, with a tall cyan outlined wordmark running vertically down the left edge and small white text over the grid ('Striker')
styles.palette: Few colours, used flat: hot pink, mustard, leaf green, violet, orange, grey-blue, bright green, plus black for text and silhouettes and white for the tag. No metallic shading.
styles.typography: Small plain pixel capitals and lower case, centred, with dotted leaders in credits; larger text is bold sans capitals in black placed on a curve. The group tag uses lower case.
styles.motion: Rings expand from the centre; curved text travels along its path as a scroller; cubes rotate. One idea per screen. Inferred from stills and comments ('It's ugly and minimal and has a scroller').

references.what: Zool cracktro by Crystal and Melon (September 1992): pink, yellow and green skyline bands with curved black text
Mind Expanding (intro, December 1993, 22nd at The Party 1993): orange rings on violet with black silhouettes
Human Target (April 1992, 1st at Easter Conference): comments on its influence on demo design
1000cc turbo cracktro (February 1992): grey-blue field, rules, green credits naming Seen for graphics and design and Tronic for music
Striker cracktro (June 1992): rainbow cube grid with vertical wordmark
Melon Dezign on Demozoo: founders, relation to Crystal and Quartex, members, productions from November 1991

styles.readme_translation: Above the fold: an animated SVG of two or three flat colour bands cut into a stepped silhouette of the project's subject (for a factory tool, a skyline of machines and chimneys), the project name and tagline as curved black text travelling across it, and a small two-tone tag in the corner for the version. It carries its own background, so it reads in both themes.
styles.feasibility_notes: Everything is flat polygons, so the file is a few KB. Curved text: letters as paths or pixel-glyph symbols, each in a group positioned along a sine with its own rotation, the whole row translated on X and duplicated to loop; SMIL animateMotion along a path with staggered begin times is the alternative. Rings are circles with SMIL-animated radius, three or four staggered for a seamless loop. Bands slide with translate keyframes. Cubes are three flat polygons each.
styles.caveats: Do not copy the melon tag, the Melon or Crystal names, or the specific silhouettes (the two figures in 'Mind Expanding'). Flat fields, rings and curved text are ordinary graphic design and free to use. Expanding high-contrast rings can be uncomfortable; keep them slow. Descriptions are from one still per production plus comments.

styles.name: Spaceballs 'State of the Art': recoloured silhouette cut out of moire rings
styles.era: 29 December 1992, Amiga OCS; 1st in the demo competition at The Party 1992
styles.what_it_is: A demo by the Norwegian group Spaceballs built around traced silhouettes of dancers cut to techno, over interference patterns and flat colour. Demozoo tags it character-animation, dance-animations, rave and epilepsy-warning, and a Pouet commenter calls it the first demo he could show to non-scene friends and get a good reaction. It is the rave-flyer end of the Amiga look, as far from copper bars as the platform gets.
visual_signature: One human silhouette, large and centred, arms spread wide, with no interior detail
A background of fine concentric rings from two offset centres whose overlap makes a moire interference pattern of crescents and swirls
The silhouette is the same ring pattern in a different colour pair: yellow and red inside the figure, green, red and violet outside, so the figure reads purely by colour change
Deliberately clashing, fully saturated colours with no outline between figure and ground
No logo, no scroller and no text on the main screens
styles.palette: High-saturation pairs: yellow and red for the figure; green, red and violet for the rings. No gradients.
styles.typography: Essentially none in the main sequence. Any title should be short, in plain heavy capitals on a flat strip.
styles.motion: The silhouette changes pose in short loops (Pouet describes rotoscoped dancers); the ring centres drift so the moire crawls; the colour scheme switches with the music. Demozoo's epilepsy-warning tag indicates fast flashing in the original. Not watched.

references.what: State of the Art on Pouet: still of the figure over moire rings, comments on the traced dancers and design
State of the Art on Demozoo: date, party placing, credits (code Lone Starr and Major Asshole, graphics TMB Designs, music Travolta), tags including epilepsy-warning
Jonathan Weinel, 'How Atari and Amiga computers shaped the design of rave culture' (OUP blog, 2018): background on these machines and rave visuals; it does not discuss this demo

styles.readme_translation: Above the fold: an animated SVG with a bold silhouette of the project's subject (for a factory tool a machine, crane or gear, not a person) recoloured out of slowly crawling moire rings, and the project name in plain heavy capitals on a solid strip at the bottom. All descriptive text goes below in Markdown.
styles.feasibility_notes: Rings: one rect filled with a radialGradient using spreadMethod="repeat" and hard colour stops gives concentric rings in a single element. Overlay a second copy with a different centre and mix-blend-mode: difference (or feComposite operator xor) for a true moire, and animate the group positions slowly with translate. Figure: draw the same two-layer ring group a second time in the other colour pair inside a clipPath of the silhouette. Pose changes are 3-4 alternative clip shapes toggled with steps() keyframes. Under 10 KB.
styles.caveats: Do not trace the original dancers or use the group name or title. Silhouette and moire are generic. Flashing is the main risk: keep colour changes below three per second, avoid red flashes, keep rings broad (fine high-contrast rings cause visual discomfort on their own), and add a prefers-reduced-motion rule that freezes it. Drawing a recognisable, original silhouette is the real work.

styles.name: 16-bit hand-pixelled chrome logo (static)
styles.era: 1988-1993, Amiga and Atari ST; drawn in Deluxe Paint at 320 pixels wide with 16 or 32 colours
styles.what_it_is: The group logo as a piece of pixel art: metal letters reflecting an imaginary sky and desert, drawn dot by dot. Damien Guard's article on Amiga lettering describes the chrome, gradient and lens-flare conventions within 16 or 32 colours, and the book 'Demoscene: The Logo Art' is devoted to logos and their makers. Named hands exist: Demozoo credits Uno with the red and blue logos and charsets in Phenomena's 'Enigma' (1991), and the Amiga Graphics Archive documents a TRSi logo by J.O.E. in 32 colours, 19 used.
visual_signature: Chrome fill split by a horizon about halfway up each letter: cool colours above (violet or deep blue to pale blue to white), a hard zigzag line, warm colours below (dark red to orange to yellow, or grey)
Banded, stepped gradients of 5-8 colours, because the whole logo shares a 16- or 32-colour palette
A one-pixel dark outline around every letter, often with a lighter inner edge to fake a bevel
A solid drop shadow or extruded side offset down and to the right
Heavy italic or slab capitals, letters touching or overlapping
Single-hue variant (Enigma): hot red to pink letters cut by thin horizontal slits with white streak highlights, beside a violet chrome wordmark with a white horizon
Composite title variant (Red Sector Megademo): a second word set vertically beside the main logo, plus a cartoon head with a speech bubble
Chrome with white sparkle stars on letter corners over a blue gradient floor (Kefrens 'Multi Megamix' title)
styles.palette: One cool ramp and one warm ramp plus black and white. Amiga colours are 12-bit, so each ramp step is one sixteenth per channel. On the ST the palette is 512 colours with 16 on screen, so ramps are shorter and coarser.
styles.typography: Custom-drawn capitals only: wide letterforms with flat tops to give room for the horizon band, light from the upper left, highlights as one-pixel white lines along top edges, sparing checkerboard dither where two bands meet.
styles.motion: Static as an image. An optional glint can travel across the letters.

references.what: Red Sector Megademo title (1989): violet top, zigzag horizon, orange-red base, vertical second word
Kefrens Megademo 8 menu logo (1990): blue to white to grey banded chrome
Enigma by Phenomena on Demozoo (30 March 1991): Uno credited for the red Enigma logo, blue logo and charsets; Imbecille for a logo; Terminator for charsets
Enigma on Pouet: stills of the red slit logo and the violet chrome wordmark
Amiga Graphics Archive: TRSi logo by J.O.E., used in TRSi's 'Time Zone' demo; lowres PAL, 32 colours, 19 used

Damien Guard, 'The Art of Amiga Lettering' (December 2025): chrome, gradients, lens flares and extrusion within 16 or 32 colours; mostly game titles, with Fairlight, Scoopex, The Silents and Enigma as demo examples
'Demoscene: The Logo Art' (Editions64K, 400 pages): logos and their makers across Amiga, Atari, C64, Amstrad, PC and consoles
Fairfax interview (Hugi 35): names Uno first among favourite graphicians for his use of colour and light within Amiga limits
Amiga Graphics Archive page for Cougar: several pictures credited as based on album-cover art, evidence for the caveat about adapted sources

styles.readme_translation: Above the fold: a static SVG of the project name as a chrome pixel logo on black, 640-800 pixels wide, optionally with a one-line subtitle in small pixel capitals. It can stand alone or sit on top of any animated style in this family.
styles.feasibility_notes: Draw letters as pixel-grid rects (run-length merged) with shape-rendering: crispEdges at 2x or 3x. Fill through a clipPath with a linearGradient that uses paired hard stops for bands; add the zigzag horizon as a polyline clipped to the letters. Dither between bands with a 2x2 checkerboard pattern. Outline and shadow are offset copies of the letter shape. Sparkles are small 4-point polygons. An optional glint is a narrow skewed white rect animated across the clip. The SVG is simple; convincing letterforms are not, and a generated logo will look mechanical beside a hand-pixelled one.
styles.caveats: Do not copy any existing group logo, the Red Sector head, or an artist's specific letterforms; the chrome recipe is common property. Artist attributions are only those stated by Demozoo and the Amiga Graphics Archive; which logo Imbecille drew in Enigma is not specified. Scene graphics of the period were often adapted from album covers and commercial art, another reason to draw from scratch. The brief also asked about 'graffiti' logos and other named logo artists; I could not source that school and have not described it.

styles.name: Atari ST menu disk: key-numbered game list, big gradient scroller, scanline rasters
styles.era: 1988-1991, Atari ST; the UK compilation scene (Automation, Medway Boys, Pompey Pirates) and the megademos whose tricks they borrowed
styles.what_it_is: On the ST, UK crackers packed several games onto one floppy and put a menu in front. Zippy of the Medway Boys made more than 100 of them, starting with menu 9, and a Pouet commenter says of Automation's intros that "there are hundreds". Each menu is a small intro with a job: list the games, say which key loads which, and scroll the news. Megademos such as The Union Demo (January 1989) and The Carebears' Cuddly Demos (July 1989) supplied the effects and the game-like main menu.
visual_signature: A short key list of the disk's contents: '1...GAME ONE, 2...GAME TWO' or 'F1: ...' to 'F4: ...', in small white or yellow capitals
Utility keys in the same block: '0...TOGGLE 50/60 HZ', 'SPACE...READ DOC FILE', 'M TO CHANGE MUSIC'
A disk number line ('DISK 10', 'CD-COMPACT NUMBER 190')
A big scroller across the bottom in letters about 32 pixels high, each filled with a vertical gradient (white to pink, or orange to red) with a dark edge
A centrepiece picture: a heavily dithered digitised photograph (a red and violet sunset sky in Pompey Pirates menu 10) or a cartoon character on a red oval (Automation 190)
A group logo in warm gradient capitals, orange to red, with a drop shadow; a second panel of grey metal with a large orange word
Full-width background gradients changed every scanline, red fading to black and back, banding in 8 steps
Megademo-menu variant: a side-view platform-game scene of brick walls and a small character above a big chrome scroller (Cuddly Demos; Automation 496 does the same with a commercial game's graphics)
styles.palette: ST low resolution: 320x200, 16 colours on screen from 512, with more by switching the palette per scanline. 8 levels per channel, so gradients band strongly. Red-to-black backgrounds, orange and yellow logos, white small text, blue and yellow accents.
styles.typography: Small text in a plain 8x8 capitals font, packed tightly at the top or bottom. Large scroller fonts are chunky capitals with a vertical gradient and a dark edge. Logos are hand-drawn slab capitals in orange and red.
styles.motion: The bottom scroller runs continuously; background rasters roll; a logo may distort line by line (commenters on Automation 190 praise the distortion); in one menu dot-built letters rotate over spinning vertical bars. The key list is static. From stills and comments.

references.what: Pompey Pirates Menu 010 (1990): key list with 50/60 Hz and doc-file keys, digitised sunset, big scroller
Automation CD #190 intro (1989; on-screen credit to Overlanders): F1-F4 list, gradient logo, character on a red oval, grey panel with large lettering
Pompey Pirates Menu 001 V2 (November 1991): red rasters, spinning vertical bars, rotating dot letters, small key list
Automation CD #496 intro (December 1990, coder EGB per comments): menu dressed as a platform-game screen
Interview with Zippy of the Medway Boys: more than 100 menus from menu 9 to 100, and how the art improved when Wizpop joined at menu 50
Pompey Pirates history by Alien: 'bigger scrollers, music, nicer graphics', and game documentation on the menus
Guido Henkel on ST graphics: 512 colours, 16 on screen, palette switched every scanline
Cuddly Demos by The Carebears (July 1989): comments on overscan, sync scrolling and the main menu
The Union Demo (January 1989): a commenter says it has the first fullscreen on the ST and started the trend of megademos with game-like main menus

styles.readme_translation: Above the fold: an animated SVG with a gradient logo, a picture or mascot panel, rolling red rasters and the big scroller. The key list maps directly to the README: '1...INSTALL, 2...USAGE, 3...RECIPES, SPACE...READ DOCS'. Put that list in real text under the image (a pre block with links) so the keys become clickable entries, and use the disk number for the version.
styles.feasibility_notes: Scanline rasters are a linearGradient with hard stops at 8 levels per channel, or a stack of 2-pixel rects; rolling them is one translateY loop. The scroller is pixel-glyph symbols clipped over a vertical gradient and translated on X. A 'digitised' picture can be faked without a bitmap by drawing flat shapes and overlaying an ordered-dither pattern; an embedded data: image is possible but heavy. The distorter is the logo cut into horizontal clip strips with staggered translateX animations. The key list is plain text.
styles.caveats: Do not copy group names, logos, or the game graphics and cartoon characters some menus lifted from commercial games. The key-list structure is generic. ST border-breaking (overscan, fullscreen) is central to the machine's demo history but means nothing in an image with no screen edge, and the walkable megademo menu needs interaction, so neither is offered as its own style. The 'first fullscreen' claim is one Pouet comment, not a settled fact. '50/60 Hz' and similar keys are jokes that need a real meaning next to them.

styles.name: Chip-music jukebox: track list with times, embossed panel, 'hit a key' legend
styles.era: 1988-1991: Atari ST (The Exceptions' B.I.G. Demo, January 1988) and Amiga music disks (Kefrens' Jukebox, 29 June 1990; Multi Megamix, November 1991)
styles.what_it_is: A screen whose whole purpose is choosing chip tunes. The B.I.G. Demo carried 113 YM2149 tunes by Jochen Hippel (Mad Max), over four hours of conversions of Rob Hubbard's C64 music, behind a menu that lists tune names with running times; Pouet commenters recall listening for hours. Amiga groups turned the idea into music disks with a drawn jukebox or a title picture. It is the closest this family gets to 'chiptune' without any sound.
visual_signature: A scrolling track list in a window: tune name on the left, duration in minutes and seconds on the right, three or four rows visible
The selected row drawn on a solid red bar, other rows in green and blue text
A 'TOP OF LIST' header above the list and key instructions below in larger lettering ('Hit 1...3 for ...', 'Hit B for the ... scroller')
ST version: a light grey embossed metal panel with title letters raised from the same grey by light and shadow edges, and round studs filled with multicolour dither
A thin strip of rainbow-coloured blocks under the legend, and scrollers running in the area beneath the panel

Amiga version (Kefrens Jukebox, graphics by Seen): a hand-pixelled jukebox with a pink-white arch, gold side columns and a brown cabinet, the current tune's title on a small display strip, party credits to the right, and a wide blue scroller band at the bottom
Amiga title-picture version (Multi Megamix): a chrome wordmark with white sparkles, red oscilloscope traces behind it, and a second chrome logo on a blue gradient floor
styles.palette: ST: mid and light greys for the panel, red for the selection, green and blue list text, a rainbow strip as the only saturated element. Amiga: black background, chrome greys, gold, pink and brown for the jukebox, blue scroller.
styles.typography: Embossed block capitals for titles; a small 8-pixel font for the list with times right-aligned; larger rounded lettering for the key legend.
styles.motion: The list scrolls when the selection moves; the selection bar steps row by row; scrollers run underneath; the rainbow strip cycles. A visual stand-in for playback (a ticking time counter, a pulsing level strip, a drawn oscilloscope trace) is the natural addition, though no level meter is visible in the stills.

references.what: The B.I.G. Demo on Pouet (The Exceptions, January 1988): main menu still with track list and times; comments about hours of listening
Microzeit on the B.I.G. Demo: 113 tunes by Jochen Hippel, over four hours, conversions of Rob Hubbard's C64 music
Wikipedia on The Exceptions: members, demo dates, '113 Tunes, 5 screens'
Kefrens 'Jukebox' music disk on Pouet (June 1990, Amiga Conference 1990): pixel jukebox with title display and scroller
Jukebox on Demozoo: 29 June 1990; Neon code, S.L.L music, Seen graphics; eight track titles
Kefrens 'Multi Megamix' (November 1991): chrome title picture with red waveform traces

styles.readme_translation: Above the fold: an animated SVG panel titled with the project name in embossed capitals, and a track list where each 'tune' is a module, command or release with a number on the right (size, count, duration). The highlighted row steps through the list and a 'now playing' line names the current item. Repeat the list as linked text below; the list with right-aligned times also works as a pre block.
styles.feasibility_notes: Emboss: three offset copies of each letter shape (light, dark, face). List: pixel-glyph rows; the selection bar is a rect moved with steps() keyframes. A ticking counter is a vertical strip of digits in a clip window stepped with steps(). A level strip is a handful of rects with scaleY keyframes at different durations. An oscilloscope trace is a polyline with 2-3 alternative point sets toggled by steps(). No sound is possible, so this only suggests music.
styles.caveats: Do not copy the demo titles, group logos, tune names or the specific jukebox drawing. A track list with times and a highlight bar is generic. The B.I.G. Demo still is small, so fine details of its panel may be off. Embossed grey-on-grey lettering is low contrast; keep list text in a strong colour. A tracker pattern view, the more familiar chiptune image, already exists in the project's cracktro style and belongs to another family.

left_out: None of the eleven submitted styles was removed. Each is distinct from the six existing styles, though two overlap them in part (the C64 crack intro with the existing 'SID title screen', the megademo menu with the existing Amiga cracktro) and are rated lower for it.

Not added as its own style: Atari ST fullscreen and border-breaking megademo screens. There is no screen edge to break in an image and the walkable menu needs interaction. The reusable parts and the Union Demo and Cuddly Demos references are folded into the ST menu-disk style.
Not added: C64 border-opening as its own style, for the same reason. It survives as an optional drawn-border variant in the DYCP style.

Not added: the 'graffiti' pixel-logo school and further named logo artists from the brief. With web search exhausted I could not reach sources that describe it; the Amiga Graphics Archive pages I opened show pictures, not logos.

Not added: shade bobs, glenz and filled vectors, and dot tunnels. Without scripts they need an accumulating buffer or many pre-computed frames. Only the dot-lattice and ball-chain forms, which reduce to sine motion, are in the bobs style.

families.title: Trackers and chiptune visuals
families.overview: Sound cannot play in a README, so this family is what module and chip music looks like on screen. After checking every reference (images were opened and looked at; three of the researcher's sampled palettes were re-measured by pixel count and matched exactly), the family holds up as eleven styles in four schools. (1) Sample trackers: the Amiga line (Ultimate Soundtracker Dec 1987, NoiseTracker 1989, ProTracker 1990/91 onward) with embossed grey panels over four black pattern windows; FastTracker II (Nov 1994) as a dense 640x400 DOS GUI; Scream Tracker 3 / Impulse Tracker / AdLib Tracker II as 80-column text-mode screens in gold, tan and navy. (2) Chip-specific trackers whose column headers are the hardware voices: LSDj on the Game Boy (160x144; PU1/PU2/WAV/NOI), GoatTracker for the three SID voices, and FamiTracker / DefleMask / Furnace with colour-coded fields. (3) Players rather than editors: Open Cubic Player's text-mode status header plus character-cell spectrum analyser, and the Winamp 2 stack. (4) YouTube-era visualisers: one oscilloscope per channel, and piano-roll / falling-note views up to black MIDI. A purely textual eleventh style, the module sample list used as a message board, was split out of the ProTracker entry because it is the only one that is native plain text. Shared grammar: a numbered row grid (NOT always hex: ProTracker, Scream Tracker 3, Impulse Tracker, GoatTracker, DefleMask and Furnace show decimal rows; FastTracker II, FamiTracker, LSDj and Cubic Player's pattern view show hex), one column per channel, a fixed highlighted play row the pattern scrolls under, and an instrument or sample list. That maps onto a repo as song title = repo name, channels = modules, sample list = dependencies or credits. One build constraint was verified directly: GitHub serves repo files from raw.githubusercontent.com with the header "Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; sandbox", so inline style blocks (and therefore CSS keyframes) are permitted but embedded data: fonts cannot be relied on and embedded data: images should be tested before use. Every pixel-font style here must therefore draw its glyphs as SVG paths (define once in defs, place with use, roughly 30-40 bytes per placed character) or accept the viewer's monospace font with textLength. None of the styles needs sound, scripts or external resources. Overlaps with the existing six to keep in mind: the Amiga cracktro style already has a tracker pattern strip, and the keygen dialog already has a spectrum analyser; the entries below say how each differs.

styles.name: Amiga 4-channel tracker (ProTracker 2.3D editor screen)
styles.era: 1987-1993, Commodore Amiga. Ultimate Soundtracker (Karsten Obarski, December 1987), NoiseTracker (Mahoney and Kaktus, 1989; its screen reads 'Northstar - Silents 1989'), ProTracker (Lars Hamre, Anders Hamre, Sven Vahsen, Rune Johnsrud; first release 1990 per its own Wikipedia page, 1991 per the Ultimate Soundtracker page). The 2.3D screen carries the line 'Noxious January 1993'.
styles.what_it_is: The editor nearly every Amiga demo, cracktro and game tune was written in: a grey embossed panel of numeric fields and buttons above four black pattern windows, one per hardware channel. It is the ancestor of every later tracker and the picture most people have in mind for 'a MOD tracker'. Distinct from the existing Amiga cracktro style, which only borrows a pattern strip: this is the whole workbench.
visual_signature: Native 320x255 screen shown at 2x (640x510). Top-left stack of nine right-aligned labels, each followed by a 4-digit field and a pair of up/down arrow buttons: POS, PATTERN, LENGTH, FINETUNE, SAMPLE, VOLUME, LENGTH, REPEAT, REPLEN (sample length shows hex such as 1E00)
A 3-column button grid to the right in wide embossed capitals: PLAY, STOP, PATTERN, CLEAR, EDIT, EDIT OP., RECORD, DISK OP., POS ED., SAMPLER, with a narrow column of 1-4 and A keys at the far right
A strip titled QUADRASCOPE over four small black windows numbered 1-4, each holding one thin yellow waveform trace
Two full-width text strips, SONGNAME: and SAMPLENAME:, the value padded to fixed length with underscores, a small LOAD button at the right end
A status strip: current pattern number in a box, tempo 125 with tiny arrows, STATUS: ALL RIGHT, and TUNE / TIMING readouts at the right

Four black pattern windows of packed 8-character cells (note letter, sharp or dash, octave, 2-digit sample, 3-digit effect, e.g. a cell shaped like F-201903), decimal row numbers 00-63 in a fifth narrow window at the far left, all in saturated blue on black
A fixed light-grey edit row across the middle with black digits, the row number enlarged in a bevelled box, and a one-cell red outline cursor
One fat vertical VU bar per channel standing on the edit row, green at the base shading to yellow (redder only near full height); a chunky yellow arrow mouse pointer
styles.palette: Re-measured from the pt2-clone screenshot by pixel count: panel grey #888888, bevel highlight #BBBBBB, bevel shadow #555555, windows #000000, pattern text blue #3344FF, scope and pointer yellow #FFDD00. The edit row is a light-grey band (#BBBBBB) with black digits, not white. Ultimate Soundtracker v1.21 variant (researcher-sampled, consistent with the image): tan #997755 panels, #AA8866 highlight, dark brown #553311 shadow, teal-blue pattern digits #006699. NoiseTracker v1.1 is the same layout in mid-grey with blue digits.
styles.typography: All-caps 8x8 bitmap face with very wide letterforms, drawn light grey with a one-pixel dark drop shadow so labels look embossed into the panel. Pattern digits are a taller, heavier numeric face. Ultimate Soundtracker labels its four channels in a thin rounded mixed-case face (Melody, Accompany, Bass, Percussions), uses +/- buttons instead of arrows, and spells the field LENGHT. NoiseTracker and Soundtracker put a logo plate (lumpy chiselled capitals; shadowed slab capitals) where ProTracker later put the scopes, and NoiseTracker has VOICE1-4: ON toggles.
styles.motion: Pattern rows step upward one row at a time under the fixed edit row; VU bars jump on each note and decay; the four scope traces wobble; POS and PATTERN counters tick at the end of a pattern; the pointer sits idle. All stepped, no easing.

references.what: pt2-clone screenshot (642x549 with window chrome): the ProTracker 2.3D pattern screen with quadrascope, VU bars, 'Noxious January 1993' line
pt2-clone repository by 8bitbubsy: states it aims to be a highly accurate clone of ProTracker 2.3D; real and fake VU meters
The Ultimate Soundtracker v1.21 screenshot: tan panels, Melody/Accompany/Bass/Percussions, LENGHT, '1987 by Karsten Obarski'
NoiseTracker v1.1 screenshot: grey variant, VOICE1-4: ON, logo plate, DISK STATUS: ALL RIGHT (the Commons file name misspells Kaktus as 'Kartus')
Wikipedia: ProTracker (authors, 'Release: 1990', MOD format, the 2.3D clone project)
Wikipedia: Ultimate Soundtracker (Obarski, December 1987; NoiseTracker 1989 by Mahoney and Kaktus; ProTracker given as 1991)
Wikipedia: Music tracker (channel labels Melody, Accompany, Bass, Percussions; chronology)

styles.readme_translation: One animated SVG at 640x510. SONGNAME carries the repo name padded with underscores; SAMPLENAME carries the tagline. The numeric fields carry real counts (LENGTH = releases, SAMPLE = dependencies, PATTERN = major version). The four channels are the project's four main modules; pattern cells are invented note data, with module names shown in a one-line label strip above the windows rather than forced into 8-character cells. Put the prose and links as ordinary Markdown below the image; pair it with the sample-list style (next entry) if a text block is wanted.
styles.feasibility_notes: All rectangles and short text. The cost is the font: define an original 8x8 glyph set as path symbols in defs and place with use. Roughly 60 panel labels, 4 x 15 visible rows x 8 characters plus row numbers = about 600 glyphs, and a looping 32-row pattern is about 1,100, so 40-60 KB total. Row stepping: a g inside a clipPath-ed parent, animated with transform: translateY and steps(n), with the first screenful of rows duplicated at the end so the loop is seamless. VU bars: keep a fixed green-to-yellow linearGradient bar and animate a black cover rect over it (scaleY on the gradient bar itself would squash the colours). Scope traces: a periodic polyline wider than its clip window, translated one period in a linear loop. Embossing is two offset copies of each glyph (dark then light), which doubles label glyph count only. Add @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) inside the SVG style to pause everything.
styles.caveats: Do not copy the ProTracker, NoiseTracker or Soundtracker logos or wordmarks, the author and group credit lines, or the song and sample names visible in the screenshots (they belong to a real, well-known module). Build an original 8x8 face rather than tracing the Amiga font bitmaps. The layout, bevel style, note notation and grid are generic and reusable. Accessibility: authentic #3344FF on black is about 3.4:1, below the 4.5:1 threshold for small text, so carry meaning in the grey-band row, the yellow and the alt text. Unconfirmed: whether the first ProTracker release was 1990 or 1991 (the two Wikipedia pages disagree); which header fields are decimal versus hex beyond what the screenshot shows. Do not make this and the cracktro's pattern strip both defaults.

styles.name: Module sample list as message board (text-only)
styles.era: 1987 onward, Amiga MOD and later XM modules; the convention was reinforced by the IntuiTracker player and is still surfaced by The Mod Archive's 'View Internal Text(s)' link
styles.what_it_is: A MOD file has a 20-character title and 31 sample slots with 22-character names, and composers routinely used the names as a notice board: credits, greetings, contact details, even block-letter pictures. Players showed this text to the listener, so the sample list became the module's own tiny NFO. It is the one tracker artefact that was always plain monospace text.
visual_signature: A title line of at most 20 characters, often lower-case with underscores or dots
31 numbered lines, each a 2-digit index followed by exactly 22 characters, so the block is a narrow column about 26 characters wide
A mix of three line types: real sample names (short lower-case words, sometimes with an st-01: style disk prefix), message lines (centred phrases, dashes and asterisks as rules), and empty slots
Message lines prefixed with # in modules written for the IntuiTracker player, which displayed # lines to the listener
Centred text padded by hand with spaces, because every slot is fixed width

In XM modules the same habit moves to the instrument list: a 'composed by' notice in the instrument names, and sometimes big block-pixel lettering built from block characters across several sample-name lines
A closing greetings or contact line in the last few slots
styles.palette: Monochrome by nature. In ProTracker the names appear as embossed grey capitals in the SAMPLENAME strip; in FastTracker II as light text on black with the selected line inverted; on The Mod Archive as plain page text. In a README it is simply the code-block colour.
styles.typography: Fixed-width, 22 characters per line, 7-bit ASCII in MOD (ProTracker shows capitals only). Decoration is limited to punctuation rules (-, =, *, #, ., _) and, in XM, block characters. Two-digit slot numbers at the left act as a ruler. A made-up example of the texture: '07 #  greets to all  #' followed by '08 bassdrum.2'.
styles.motion: static

references.what: MOD format specification: 20-byte song name, 31 samples with 22-byte names, 64 rows x 4 channels, and the note that sample names are often used for author messages, with # lines shown by the IntuiTracker player
The Mod Archive module page with the 'View Internal Text(s)' link, showing the tradition is still exposed to listeners
ft2-clone screenshot in which the instrument list holds a centred 'composed by' notice and the sample list holds block-pixel lettering (look at the technique, do not copy the content)
FastTracker II v2.06 screenshot: numbered instrument list 01-08 with st-01: prefixed names

styles.readme_translation: A single <pre> block, above the fold, about 26-60 columns wide: line 1 is the repo name as the song title, then 31 numbered slots. Real dependencies or modules sit in some slots as if they were samples; the rest spell out the tagline, install command, licence and greetings in the hand-centred style. Links work inside <pre>, so dependency names and the docs pointer can be real anchors. Two lists side by side (instruments = features, samples = dependencies) fill 80 columns. It also works as the caption block under the ProTracker or FastTracker SVG.
styles.feasibility_notes: Pure ASCII, no box-drawing required, well under 80 columns, renders identically on web and mobile. The generator only has to pad or truncate each entry to 22 characters and centre message lines. If block-pixel lettering is wanted, use the full block and half blocks (U+2588, U+2580, U+2584), which are in GitHub's code fonts; keep it to 22 columns so it still reads as a sample list.
styles.caveats: Do not reuse any real module's title, sample names, composer credits or messages: invent the content. The slot structure, the numbering and the # convention are format facts and free to use. Screen readers will read 31 numbered lines one by one, so keep the essential facts (name, one-line description, install) in ordinary Markdown as well. Unconfirmed: I did not open the internal-text view of a specific module (only the page that links to it), so the description of typical message content rests on the spec's wording and the one XM screenshot.

styles.name: FastTracker II (dense DOS GUI tracker with scope grid)
styles.era: November 1994 to 1997/98, MS-DOS, by Fredrik 'Mr. H' Huss and Magnus 'Vogue' Hogdahl of the demogroup Triton (Wikipedia: last stable 2.08 in August 1997, 2.09 beta leaked 1998; Demozoo lists 2.09 in August 1998). Continued by 8bitbubsy's ft2-clone and by MilkyTracker, which says it attempts to recreate FT2's replay and user experience.
styles.what_it_is: The tracker that carried the mid-1990s PC demoscene and introduced the XM format (up to 32 channels). It took ProTracker's arrangement and turned it into a mouse-driven 640x400 screen crammed with small bevelled buttons, a grid of numbered scopes and an instrument list. Tracker chiptunes in this lineage were commonly reused in keygens because the files are tiny.
visual_signature: The whole 640x400 screen divided into panels by single-pixel pale cyan frame lines on a teal-grey ground
Top-left: a song position list of paired 2-digit hex values in a black box with Ins. / Del. buttons, then Songlen. and Repstart counters

A logo plate: a heavy, upright, blocky mixed-case wordmark in white with a dark shadow over a two-tone checker band, with a tiny credit plate at its right; beneath it BPM, Spd., Add., Ptn., Ln. counters with pairs of tiny arrow buttons and Expd. / Srnk. buttons
A status strip reading free memory and a Time counter (Avail ...k, Time 00:00:44)

Two columns of narrow grey bevelled text buttons: About, Nibbles, Zap, Extend, Transps., I.E.Ext., S.E.Ext., Adv. Edit, Add/Sub and Play sng., Play ptn., Stop, Rec. sng., Rec. ptn., Disk op., Instr. Ed., Smp. Ed., Config, Help
A grid of small scope cells, numbered in the top-left corner from 0 (8 cells in two rows of four, or up to 24-32 in narrower rows), black with a thin pale-yellow trace and a tiny REC tag

Right side: an instrument list numbered 01-08 with the selected line inverted, a column of range buttons (01-08, 09-10, 11-18 ... 39-40), a shorter sample list numbered 00-04 with a scrollbar, and a Swap Bank button

Lower half: the pattern editor, hex row numbers on both edges, 8 channel columns headed by their number, cells as note, instrument, volume, effect with empty fields drawn as rows of tiny dots, and a full-width highlighted band for the current row
styles.palette: Two real schemes, researcher-sampled and consistent with the screenshots. Default v2.06: black #000000, desktop and panels teal-grey #497582, button face grey #9E9E9E, dark frame #18282C, frame lines pale cyan #8ADBF3, pattern text pale yellow #FFFF82, white #FFFFFF. Blue scheme (the English Wikipedia screenshot): panels #285586, buttons #9696B6, lines and text #9ED3FF, accents #4996EB, shadows #102034, pattern text white.
styles.typography: A proportional bitmap UI face with rounded bold lower-case letters for buttons and labels (abbreviations end in a full stop: Spd., Ptn., Smp. Ed.), plus a separate compact fixed-width pattern face in which notes read like E-4 or D#5 and empty fields are low dots. The wordmark is upright and blocky, not italic. Hex for row numbers, order positions and instrument ranges.
styles.motion: Every scope cell draws a live waveform; the pattern scrolls under the fixed centre row; the position list highlight and the Time counter advance. The About and Nibbles buttons (Nibbles is a built-in snake game) suggest an easter-egg frame.

references.what: Wikipedia: FastTracker 2 (authors, November 1994, 2.08 August 1997, layout description, Nibbles, XM, 32 channels)
